anf_compare.notes: Translated from the PG 74 Greek; no published English version was used for wording.

choices.why: ‘The mystical blessing’ (μυστικὴ εὐλογία) is Cyril’s usual term for the Eucharist; kept literal in the reading text.
‘Fervent in spirit’ (ζέοντος τῷ πνεύματι) is a verbal echo of Romans 12:11 and is cited as an allusion.
‘Holy from the womb’ (ἅγιος ἐκ μήτρας) may echo Luke 1:35; uncertain, so not cited inline.

pass_a_gloss: [continuing ‘likeness of flesh of sin’] …resembling (προσεοικός) our bodies, yet not knowing to be sick with fleshly uncleanness (ἀκαθαρσία); for holy from the womb (ἐκ μήτρας) that divine temple (νεώς). As far as it came to the notions and principles (λόγοι) in nature, none would shrink from saying that, since it was flesh (σάρξ), it would have had its own and innate motion (ἔμφυτον κίνημα). But since the Word sanctifying (ἁγιάζων) all creation has indwelt (κατῴκηκεν) it, condemned (κατακέκριται) is sin's power, so that the achievement (κατωρθωμένον) passes also to us; for we have partaken of him spiritually and bodily; for when Christ lodges (ἐναυλίζηται) in us through the Holy Spirit and through the mystical blessing (μυστικὴ εὐλογία), then wholly in us too the law of sin is condemned. True therefore: the impossible of the law (τὸ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου), in which it was weak (ἠσθένει) through the flesh, has ceased through Christ having condemned and abolished (κατηργηκότος) sin in the flesh, that the ordinance (δικαίωμα) of the law be fulfilled in us; fulfilled is the ordinance, i.e. the power of things decreed by the law, i.e. the will looking to virtue (ἀρετή), the law in us in no way, as I said, still weak through being tyrannized (τυραννεῖσθαι) by innate pleasures. Fulfilled then in us, who walk not by flesh but wish to live spiritually. Lemma: the mind (φρόνημα) of the flesh death, mind of Spirit life and peace. He says rightly flesh-mind is death, that of spirit life and peace; for love-of-flesh (φιλοσαρκία) truly the procurer (πρόξενος) of death, of life eternal and goods above the choosing to live spiritually; for if flesh-mind is enmity (ἔχθρα) to God, as not enduring to yield to divine laws, nor can it — how will foul and profane pleasure please God? — wholly the mind pure of filth and passions, as far as possible to man's nature, is at peace (εἰρηνεύει) toward God. Lemma: those in flesh cannot please God; you not in flesh but in spirit, if Spirit of God dwells in you. Earthy pleasure prevailing over man's thought, one is in flesh as minding the flesh's things; such would not please God; mind having become rich (καταπλουτήσαντος) in grace through Christ, filled with power from above, boiling (ζέοντος) in spirit, hastening to virtue, such is thought not in flesh but in spirit, and easily does things pleasing to God. Lemma: if one has not Spirit of Christ, he is not his. If one is in spirit, he will be in righteousness and life, the body of sin all but dead (μονονουχὶ τεθνεῶτος) and every unseemly pleasure quenched; impossible in the same and at one time righteousness and unrighteousness, sanctification and uncleanness. Spirit we say the human; in ‘the spirit is life’, made alive (ζωοποιούμενον) by the Holy Spirit's grace and by communion (κοινωνία) toward it being rich [in — continues next section].
pass_b_english: …to our bodies, yet not prone to the sickness of fleshly impurity; for that divine temple was holy from the womb.
As far as the concepts and principles that belong to nature are concerned, no one would hesitate to say that, since it was flesh, it would have had in itself its own innate movement.
But since the Word who sanctifies the whole creation made his dwelling in it, the power of sin has been condemned, so that what was achieved might pass over to us as well.

For we have shared in him both spiritually and bodily: when Christ comes to dwell in us too, through the Holy Spirit and through the mystical blessing, then surely the law of sin is condemned in us as well.

It is true, then, that the law’s inability, in that it was weak through the flesh, has ceased through Christ, who condemned and abolished sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us (Romans 8:3-4).

For the just requirement of the law has been fulfilled, that is, the force of what the law decreed, namely the will that looks toward virtue, since the law within us is, as I said, in no way weak any longer through being tyrannized by innate pleasures.
So the just requirement of the law has been fulfilled in us who do not walk according to the flesh (Romans 8:4) but wish rather to live spiritually.
For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace (Romans 8:6).

He says, and quite rightly, that the mind of the flesh is death, while that of the spirit is life and peace. For love of the flesh truly brings about death, whereas the choice to live one’s life spiritually brings about life everlasting and the good things from above.

For if the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God (Romans 8:7), since it does not bear to yield to the divine laws—indeed it cannot, for how could a foul and profane pleasure please God?—then surely the mind that is clean of filth and passions is at peace with God, so far as human nature allows.
Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you (Romans 8:8-9).
When earthly pleasure prevails over a person’s understanding, he is in the flesh, as one who sets his mind on the things of the flesh; and such a one could not please God.

But when the mind has grown rich in the grace that comes through Christ, is filled with strength from above, is fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11), and hastens toward virtue, such a person is understood to be not in the flesh but in the spirit, and readily does what is pleasing to God.
Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9).

If, then, anyone is in the spirit, he will also be in righteousness and in life, since the body of sin is all but dead and every unseemly pleasure has been quenched. For righteousness and unrighteousness, holiness and impurity, cannot exist in the same person at one and the same time.

By “spirit” we mean the human spirit; and in the words “the spirit is life” (Romans 8:10), we mean the spirit given life by the grace of the Holy Spirit and enriched, through its communion with him, …

ἡμετέροις σώμασιν, οὐ μὴν ἔτι καὶ νοσεῖν εἰδὸς σαρκικὴν ἀκαθαρσίαν· ἅγιος γὰρ ἐκ
μήτρας ὁ θεῖος ἐκεῖνος νεώς. καὶ ὅσον μὲν ἧκεν εἰς ἐννοίας τε καὶ λόγους τοὺς ἐν τῇ
φύσει, κατοκνήσειεν ἂν οὐδεὶς ἐκεῖνο εἰπεῖν, ὡς ἐπείπερ ἦν σὰρξ, ἔσχεν ἂν ἐν ἑαυτῇ τὸ
ἴδιόν τε καὶ ἔμφυτον κίνημα· ἐπειδὴ δὲ ὁ πᾶσαν τὴν κτίσιν ἁγιάζων Λόγος κατῴκηκεν
ἐν αὐτῇ, κατακέκριται τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἡ δύναμις, ἵνα καὶ εἰς ἡμᾶς διαβαίνῃ τὸ
κατωρθωμένον· μετεσχήκαμεν γὰρ αὐτοῦ πνευματικῶς τε καὶ σωματικῶς· ὅταν γὰρ καὶ
ἡμῖν ἐναυλίζηται Χριστὸς διὰ τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματος καὶ διὰ τῆς μυστικῆς εὐλογίας, τότε
δὴ πάντως καὶ ἐν ἡμῖν ὁ τῆς ἁμαρτίας κατακρίνεται νόμος. Ἀληθὲς οὖν ὅτι τὸ ἀδύνατον
τοῦ νόμου ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς πέπαυται διὰ Χριστοῦ κατακρίναντός τε καὶ
κατηργηκότος τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ ἵνα τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου πληρωθῇ ἐν ἡμῖν·
πεπλήρωται γὰρ τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου, τουτέστιν ἡ δύναμις τῶν τεθεσπισμένων διὰ
τοῦ νόμου, ἤγουν τὸ θέλημα τὸ βλέπον εἰς ἀρετὴν, τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν ὄντος νόμου κατ' οὐδένα
τρόπον ὡς ἔφην ἀσθενοῦντος ἔτι διὰ τοῦ τυραννεῖσθαι ταῖς ἐμφύτοις ἡδοναῖς.
πεπλήρωται τοίνυν ἐν ἡμῖν τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου τοῖς μὴ κατὰ σάρκα περιπατοῦσι,
ζῆν δὲ μᾶλλον ἐθέλουσι πνευματικῶς. Τὸ γὰρ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς θάνατος, τὸ δὲ
φρόνημα τοῦ Πνεύματος ζωὴ καὶ εἰρήνη. Θάνατον μὲν εἶναί φησι τὸ τῆς σαρκὸς
φρόνημα, καὶ μάλα ὀρθῶς· τὸ δέ γε τοῦ πνεύματος, ζωὴν καὶ εἰρήνην· θανάτου μὲν γὰρ
ἀληθῶς ἡ φιλοσαρκία πρόξενος· ζωῆς δὲ τῆς εἰς αἰῶνα καὶ τῶν ἄνωθεν ἀγαθῶν, τὸ
διαβιοῦν ἑλέσθαι πνευματικῶς· εἰ γὰρ τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς Θεὸν, ὡς 214
οὐκ ἀνεχόμενον τοῖς θείοις ὑπείκειν νόμοις, οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται· πῶς γὰρ ἀρέσει Θεῷ
μυσαρὰ καὶ βέβηλος ἡδονή; πάντως ὁ καθαρὸς ῥύπου καὶ παθῶν νοῦς κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν

17

τῇ ἀνθρώπου φύσει πρὸς Θεὸν εἰρηνεύει. Οἱ δὲ ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντες Θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται·
ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐν σαρκὶ ἀλλ' ἐν πνεύματι, εἴπερ Πνεῦμα Θεοῦ οἰκεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν.
Ἐπικρατούσης μὲν τῆς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου διανοίας τῆς γεώδους ἡδονῆς, ἐν σαρκί τις ἐστὶν
ὡς τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς φρονῶν· καὶ ὁ τοιοῦτος οὐκ ἂν ἀρέσῃ Θεῷ· καταπλουτήσαντος δὲ τοῦ
νοῦ τὴν διὰ Χριστοῦ χάριν, καὶ τῆς ἄνωθεν ἰσχύος μεμεστωμένου, καὶ ζέοντος τῷ
πνεύματι, καὶ ἐπὶ ἀρετὴν σπεύδοντος· οὐ νοεῖται ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐν σαρκὶ ἀλλ' ἐν πνεύματι,
καὶ εὐκόλως ποιεῖ τὰ ἀρεστὰ τῷ Θεῷ. Εἰ δέ τις Πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ οὐκ ἔχει, οὗτος οὐκ ἔστιν
αὐτοῦ. Εἴ τις οὖν ἐστιν ἐν πνεύματι, οὗτος ἔσται καὶ ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ἐν ζωῇ,
μονονουχὶ τεθνεῶτος τοῦ τῆς ἁμαρτίας σώματος καὶ πάσης ἀτόπου σβεσθείσης ἡδονῆς·
ἀδύνατον γὰρ ἐν ταὐτῷ καὶ καθ' ἕνα καιρὸν δικαιοσύνην εἶναι καὶ ἀδικίαν, ἁγιασμόν τε
καὶ ἀκαθαρσίαν. πνεῦμα δέ φαμεν τὸ ἀνθρώπινον· ἐν δὲ τῷ Τὸ πνεῦμα ζωὴ, τῇ τοῦ
Ἁγίου Πνεύματος ζωοποιούμενον χάριτι, καὶ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ κοινωνίᾳ πλουτοῦν
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Staged new row, reviewed clause by clause against the PG Greek. (1) Ἀληθὲς οὖν ὅτι τὸ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου … πέπαυται: Cyril is confirming the sentence he reconstructed in u06-rem-early, so it now reads 'the law’s inability … has ceased', matching u06-open and u06-rem-early, instead of a different wording ('what the law could not do … brought to an end'). (2) ἤγουν means 'that is / namely', not 'or rather'. (3) ἐθέλουσι is 'wish', not 'choose' (modality). (4) Divine pronouns lowercased (his/him) to match the book's live rows and the adjacent u06-open / u06-rem-early / u07-rem-early. Scripture refs (Romans 8:3-4, 8:6-10, 12:11) checked; no omissions or additions.

Opens mid-sentence: the clause continues the gloss on ‘the likeness of sinful flesh’ (Romans 8:3) begun at the end of u06-rem-early (προσεοικὸς μὲν τοῖς | ἡμετέροις σώμασιν); the leading ellipsis marks the join.

Closes mid-sentence: πλουτοῦν governs δικαιοσύνην, the first word of u06-rem-close; the trailing ellipsis marks the join. Cyril quotes Romans 8:10 only as ‘the spirit is life’; his gloss runs on into u06-rem-close (‘…with righteousness’).
‘The mystical blessing’ (μυστικὴ εὐλογία) is Cyril’s usual term for the Eucharist; kept literal in the reading text.
‘Fervent in spirit’ (ζέοντος τῷ πνεύματι) is a verbal echo of Romans 12:11 and is cited as an allusion.
Capitalization follows the PG text for the lemmas: ‘Spirit’ where Πνεῦμα denotes the Holy Spirit; ‘spirit’ where Cyril says he means the human spirit (πνεῦμα δέ φαμεν τὸ ἀνθρώπινον).
‘Holy from the womb’ (ἅγιος ἐκ μήτρας) may echo Luke 1:35; uncertain, so not cited inline.
PG page number 214 and Khazarzar page marker 17 in the source block are not text and are omitted.
